summary:
Missouri law makes state identity documents effectively unavailable to a transgender visitor who has not had surgery. Under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9), changing the sex on a Missouri birth certificate requires a court order supported by certified proof on hospital letterhead, including the attending physician's licensing and contact information, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible. The original certificate has the old name and gender struck through and the abstract marked amended. Two earlier cases, 13AR-CV00157 and 13AR-CV00240, which had allowed exceptions, were reversed in May 2022, leaving no route around the surgical requirement.

Driver's licences and state identification follow a separate and unstable path. Between 2016 and 2024 the Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 to change the gender designation after a policy review; the department then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order, a change the sources attribute to an unspecified incident.

Health care for minors is banned. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 and bars under-18s from starting hormones or puberty blockers, permits those already in treatment to continue, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors. The same law bars MO HealthNet, the state Medicaid programme, from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, and it restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres. Providers who violate it can lose their Missouri medical licence and can be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment. The ban carries a sunset of 28 August 2027.

The ban has survived every court test so far. A preliminary injunction was denied and the law took effect as scheduled; after a September 2024 trial in the 44th Judicial Circuit Court, Judge Robert Craig Carter upheld it as constitutional on 25 November 2024, and the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously affirmed on 13 January 2026, citing the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's equivalent ban. The plaintiffs, represented by Lambda Legal and the ACLU of Missouri, said they would appeal. Lawmakers have introduced legislation to make the ban permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to ban the care indefinitely.

Adults are not covered by the minor ban, but the state has attempted to restrict adult care. In April 2023 the attorney general issued an emergency order declaring adult gender-affirming care experimental and requiring three years of documented intense dysphoria, at least 15 psychiatric sessions over 18 months with at least 10 with the same therapist, full treatment of comorbidities, autism screening, 15-year adverse-effect tracking, annual dysphoria assessment, screening for social contagion, written consent every three months for three years and then every six months, and detailed compliance records. A judge temporarily blocked the order and the attorney general withdrew it in May 2023, along with separate March and April 2023 emergency orders on youth care that had imposed social media addiction screening, consent and dysphoria assessment requirements.

Custody is a documented site of exposure. The SAFE Act restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and an appropriations law signed by Governor Mike Kehoe, HB 2009, took effect on 2 July 2026, barring state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care.

The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations and of complaints about a "gender transition intervention," which gives residents and staff a channel to report transgender people and their providers.

Statewide protections are thin. Missouri's non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity, so there is no statewide protection in employment, housing or public accommodations; a 2010 executive order extends sexual orientation protections to state government employees only. The hate crime statute does explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender." Kansas City declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals and rights in May 2023, and Columbia voted in February 2024 to add LGBT protections to its sanctuary ordinance.

Missouri recognises marriages between people of the same sex. Out-of-state marriages were recognised from November 2013 under an executive order on joint tax filing upheld in Barrier v. Vasterling on 3 October 2014; St. Louis city and county and Jackson County began licensing such marriages after State of Missouri v. Florida and Lawson v. Kelly in November 2014, and a July 2015 executive order directed state agencies to comply.
tangentialFactors:
Missouri became the seventh U.S. state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban gender-affirming care for inmates. Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while similar Idaho and Georgia measures were blocked by federal courts.

The attorney general said in May 2023 that he did not know the difference between the civil and criminal penalties attached to the health-care ban before the governor signed it, which bears on how the penalties were understood at enactment.

A 2021 law, SB53, reduced Missouri's 1980s-era HIV criminalisation provisions from a felony to a misdemeanour.
localsOnly:
Senate Bill 39, enacted in May 2023, bars transgender athletes from female sports in public and private schools through college, and carries a sunset of 28 August 2027.

Missouri adoption law under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 453.010 does not limit adoption based on LGBT status, and there is no explicit prohibition on same-sex or second-parent adoption as of 2009.

Domestic partnership registries in Clayton, Columbia, Jackson County, Kansas City, Olivette, St. Louis and University City provide certain benefits within their borders for both opposite-sex and same-sex couples.

Non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity. A 2010 executive order provides sexual orientation protections for state government employees, and a 2013 bill banning sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations passed the Senate 19-11 but died when the House adjourned without considering it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources differ on the date the preliminary injunction was denied, giving August 2023 in one account and August 2024 in another; the law has been in force since 28 August 2023 either way.

The incident behind the Department of Revenue's reversal on licence gender designation is not described.

Whether the November 2026 ballot initiative qualifies for the ballot, and its outcome, is not sourced.

Whether the legislature will make the ban permanent before the 28 August 2027 sunset is unresolved.

The number of reports made to the tipline and any investigations or prosecutions arising from it are not sourced.

Whether the Idaho and Georgia inmate-care measures remain blocked is not sourced beyond the initial ruling.

Whether the SAFE Act's restriction on treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres has been applied, and how, is not sourced.
